issues.legal_issue: Estate duty paid in respect of inherited property is not deductible as the cost of acquiring or improving the property when payment does not acquire an additional interest or improve the recipient’s title.
material_facts: The properties passed first to an heir by succession and later to the assessee under a will.
Estate duty was payable in respect of the estates, and the duty payable in respect of immovable property was a first charge on that property.
The assessee had become the full owner of the properties before paying the estate duty attributable to the properties later transferred.
Payment of the duty did not give the assessee a new right in the properties or improve an incomplete or imperfect title.
issues.conclusion: The proportionate estate duty paid in respect of the transferred properties could not be deducted as either cost of acquisition or cost of improvement in computing capital gains.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 48, 49 and 55 of the Income Tax Act permit deductions for cost of acquisition and cost of improvement; section 49 carries forward the previous owner’s acquisition cost in specified modes of transfer. Sections 53 and 74 of the Estate Duty Act make the recipient accountable for duty, subject to the stated limit, and create a charge on the relevant property. Under section 100 of the Transfer of Property Act, a charge does not itself transfer an interest in the property or reduce full ownership to limited ownership. Applying Dattatraya Shanker Mote v. Anand Chintaman Datar and State Bank of Bikaner & Jaipur v. National Iron & Steel Rolling Corporation, the Court held that the charge gives priority in recovery but does not make the recipient’s title incomplete. Because payment neither acquired a further interest nor improved title, it was not deductible under sections 48 and 55. The Court also explained that Winans v. Attorney General concerned the incidence of estate duty and did not resolve whether a charge creates an interest in property.

issues.legal_issue: A new, independent diversion-of-income argument that was not considered by the fact-finding or High Court proceedings cannot be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court in the appeal.
material_facts: The assessee’s arguments before the Tribunal and the High Court sought deduction as cost of acquisition or cost of improvement.
The diversion argument was raised for the first time before the Supreme Court.
The Tribunal and the High Court had not considered whether a deduction for diversion was available apart from the express deductions in the capital-gains provisions.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the diversion argument because it was an independent issue raised for the first time at that stage.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the diversion argument as an independent issue outside the contentions considered by the Tribunal and the High Court, and declined to examine it for the first time in the Supreme Court appeal. No earlier case was relied on for this procedural ruling.

predicates.independent_diversion_argument: The appellant advances a theory that income should be excluded by diversion, independently of the deductions previously claimed.

issues.definition: In a capital-gains tax appeal, when an independent diversion theory is first raised before the Supreme Court and was not considered below, the Court does not consider it.

issues.legal_issue: Payment by an heir to discharge a mortgage created by the previous owner and subsisting when the property is inherited is deductible as the cost of acquiring the mortgagee’s interest.
material_facts: The Court considered the situation of property inherited while still subject to a mortgage created by the previous owner.
The heir pays the mortgage debt after inheriting the property, thereby clearing the mortgage and acquiring the mortgagee’s interest in the property.
The Court rejected the contrary approach in Ambat Echukutty Menon and approved the view in Commissioner of Income Tax v. Daksha Ramanlal.
issues.conclusion: The amount paid by an heir to clear a mortgage created by the previous owner and subsisting at inheritance is deductible as cost of acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 48, 49 and 55(2) of the Income Tax Act, the payment is cost of acquiring the mortgagee’s interest because a mortgage transfers an interest in property and the heir initially inherits only the mortgagor’s interest. The Court held that Ambat Echukutty Menon v. Commissioner of Income Tax failed to account for that transfer of interest and approved Commissioner of Income Tax v. Daksha Ramanlal.

issues.legal_issue: A property owner’s payment to discharge a mortgage the owner created after acquiring the property is not deductible as the cost of acquiring or improving the property.
material_facts: The Court distinguished a mortgage created by a previous owner from one created by the owner after acquiring the property.
It stated that when the owner created the mortgage after acquiring the property, discharging it before transfer acquired no further interest in the property.
issues.conclusion: Payment to discharge a mortgage created by the owner after acquiring the property does not qualify for deduction in computing capital gains.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 48, 49 and 55 of the Income Tax Act, the discharge of a mortgage created by the owner after acquisition does not represent the acquisition of a further property interest, unlike an heir’s payment to clear a mortgage that the previous owner created and that subsisted at inheritance.
